abstract: Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall–compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.

sections.body: The introduction defines State Integrity Collapse (SIC) as a model that recovers a constraint under probe but fails to make it govern the next answer, and separates this from ordinary forgetting. It presents StateTrack-Bench, with numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. The reported findings are that strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, that symbolic constraints degrade faster than factual-memory bindings, and that 88.6% of observed failures are integrity failures. The core benchmark has 125 scenario-depth probes per model, giving 875 primary scored outputs. The extended and cross-lingual pilots are treated as supporting evidence, not as proof that all current models collapse uniformly.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Models can restate a constraint yet stop applying it, and the paper measures this gap across dialogue depth.

sections.body: The related-work section compares the study with instruction-following benchmarks, task-oriented dialogue corpora such as MultiWOZ and SGD, and long-context evaluations. It argues that slot-filling works over a closed, task-specific ontology, while the paper's constraints are open-domain and span format, style, content, and persona. Dialogue state tracking benchmarks evaluate state tracking separately from generation, whereas this design requires recall and compliance in the same generated output. Long-context work is extended from retrieval to compliance, since information may be verbally recoverable yet fail to control generation. Agent-memory benchmarks are described as focusing on recoverability or tool-mediated use, and the benchmark is positioned as a diagnostic rather than a red-teaming tool.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work covers instruction following, dialogue state tracking, and long-context position effects, but not whether remembered constraints stay binding.

sections.body: Each dialogue has a setup phase where the user states a persistent constraint, a distractor phase of related but non-identical requests, and a test phase where the model must answer under the constraint. A judge assigns a binary label J, where 1 means the output satisfies both the immediate request and the persistent constraint. Strict joint retention is averaged over the five categories and the turn depths 3, 5, 7, 10, and 12. Early-to-late decay is the difference between retention at turn 3 and turn 12. The forked audit defines SIC+ as the share of probes where the model recalls the constraint but the compliance branch fails, and SIC- as the reverse. Scoring is conservative, and numerical and format constraints use deterministic checks where possible.
sections.heading: Benchmark and Metrics
sections.headline: Strict joint retention counts a response only when it meets both the immediate request and the persistent constraint.

sections.body: Seven snapshots are tested: GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Claude-Sonnet-4-6, Gemini-3.1-Pro, DeepSeek-v4-Pro, DeepSeek-v4-Flash, and Qwen3.6-Plus. Decoding is deterministic, and prompts, judge prompts, and random seeds are fixed. Logged endpoint identifiers are listed in Table 1, and the authors note that closed-provider names may drift. Model comparisons use paired bootstrap tests. The primary judge is GPT-5.4 at temperature 0, and it receives the full dialogue history, the active constraint, and the response. A stratified 200-output subset was re-scored by Claude-Sonnet-4-6 and Gemini-3.1-Pro, giving a Fleiss' kappa of 0.89 across the three judges. Distractor turns were checked for lexical overlap with the constraint using a Jaccard threshold below 0.05.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Seven provider-pinned model snapshots are tested at fixed prompts and seeds, with a single GPT-5.4 judge.

sections.body: DeepSeek-v4-Flash reaches 100.0% overall, followed by GPT-5.4-mini at 98.4% and DeepSeek-v4-Pro at 96.0%. Gemini-3.1-Pro averages 62.4%, with a drop of 10.0 points from turn 3 to turn 12. In the category means of Table 4, factual-memory retention is 95.4 and logical-rule retention is 83.5. In the forked audit, 88.6% of observed failures are integrity failures, with a Wilson 95% interval of 79.7 to 93.9. Excluding Gemini-3.1-Pro, the integrity share is 84.4%. Gemini-3.1-Pro contributes 47 of the 79 failures. Reinstatement gives full recovery in 53.2% to 100% of collapsed scenarios, but the paper states that it does not erase the underlying collapse.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: DeepSeek-v4-Flash scores 100.0% strict joint retention while Gemini-3.1-Pro falls to 62.4% and loses 10.0 points by turn 12.

sections.body: Manual inspection finds failures that keep an explicit reference to the instruction while violating its operational content, such as an unsolicited preface after a format acknowledgment. Three evaluators re-scored 120 outputs, and their majority vote agreed with the automated judge on 93.3%. Disagreements concentrated in role/persona items (4.2%) and logical-rule items (2.5%), where the automated judge was stricter. Distractor turns had a mean Jaccard similarity of 0.040 with the constraint, and a mean naturalness rating of 4.2 with standard deviation 0.6. A 216-probe analysis over six models gives compliance of 94.4%, 95.8%, and 90.3% at depths 12, 30, and 50. At depth 50, five of six models show at least one recalled-but-violated case.
sections.heading: Analysis
sections.headline: Excluding Gemini-3.1-Pro, numerical constraints at depth 50 show 100.0% recall but 79.2% compliance.

sections.body: Errors differ by constraint type. Numerical and format constraints fail through loss of exact surface form, role/persona constraints give way to a generic assistant voice, and logical rules fail when follow-ups change their scope. The extended-depth pilot shows divergence at turns 20 to 50 for three models, but the paper does not claim a common decay curve. The cross-lingual pilot suggests the dissociation is not specific to English. Structured State Anchoring with prepending alone recovers 62% of lost compliance at a cost of +13% tokens. In a dynamic-state audit, stale anchoring enforces a superseded rule in 74.3% of cases, while updating the ledger reduces stale enforcement to 0.0%. Deployment systems therefore need an explicit update policy before re-anchoring.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Symbolic constraints fail silently, so retrieval alone is insufficient and monitoring should prioritize them.

sections.body: The conclusion states that StateTrack-Bench shows persistent-state evaluation is necessary for multi-turn reliability. It defines State Integrity Collapse as a recalled constraint that fails to govern generation. It says this failure type remains dominant after excluding the most brittle model. The section is brief and introduces no new numbers, so its claims rest on the results reported in earlier sections.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Persistent-state evaluation is necessary, since State Integrity Collapse remains the dominant failure even without the most brittle model.

sections.body: The core benchmark has 125 probes per model, with 25 per category, which limits within-category inference. The judges are model-based, with a Fleiss kappa of 0.89 across three judges, and larger-scale human evaluation is future work. The cross-lingual pilot covers 30 scenarios and is described as a diagnostic signal rather than a definitive estimate. Finnish, Turkish, and Arabic are untested. Distractors are cooperative, so adversarial override is not measured. The extended pilot uses a 40-scenario subset, and multi-session settings beyond depth 50 remain future work. Each dialogue has one persistent constraint, and the anchoring mitigation may over-enforce a stale rule without an update detector.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Limits include 25 probes per category, model-based judging, a 30-scenario pilot, cooperative distractors, and one constraint per dialogue.

sections.body: All scenario dialogues were authored by the research team, and the paper states they contain no personally identifiable information, offensive content, or material that could cause harm. The benchmark does not involve human subjects in the traditional sense. Crowdwork annotators were paid USD 18 per hour, which the paper says is above the local minimum wage. The benchmark is released under CC BY 4.0, which the paper says permits commercial use for safety evaluation. The main stated ethical risk is misuse of the results as a blanket ranking of model safety. The authors say the findings should be read as a targeted audit of persistent constraint adherence, not a comprehensive safety evaluation.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: Scenarios were team-authored with no personal data, and the main risk is misuse as a blanket model safety ranking.

sections.body: Appendix A gives dataset composition, with 125 scenarios across five categories and an average of 55.4 tokens, and a three-way annotation protocol with Fleiss kappa of 0.91 for numerical and 0.79 for role/persona. Appendix C gives case studies, including the finding that numerical predicates inside logical rules account for 63% of logical-rule failures. Appendix D reports percentile bootstrap intervals with 10,000 resamples and a Cohen's d of 3.2 between the highest and lowest models. Appendix E reports a maximum temperature shift of 2.1 points. Appendices F and G report extended-depth and cross-lingual pilots. Appendices H to L cover state anchoring, dynamic-state audits, judge checks, inference cost, and prompt sensitivity, with a maximum prompt-variant deviation of 3.6 points.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, confidence intervals, temperature and prompt-variant checks, pilots, state anchoring costs, judge audits, and release details.
